messages.subject: Fwd: Re: BUGS Model Performance
parts:
I'm attaching Michael's output plots.

The executive summary is that the results are still way off
in most of the BUGS models.

Michael --- does your calculation of R-hat and effective sample
size match bin/print and RStan?

Why is the overall frequency of v1.3.0 samples so much lower?
These plots would be much easier to read if they involved the same
number of iterations for both systems.
(Are you sure you're throwing away the warmup iterations for
the new stuff and also including all the multiple chains for v1.3.0?)

For many of the test cases, the accuracies are comparable. But
for many, they're not and in all the incomparable cases, the new code
looks much much worse in terms of accuracy vs. known values.
Oddly, the time per effective sample is much lower in the
new code. Something seems to be fishy.

I'd be inclined to start debugging with Rats, because it's a very
simple model and both systems think they've converged, but the new
implementation is way off in its estimates for a whole batch of
the parameters.

I'm particularly bothered by lsat, which has low R-hat values,
but very far off estimates.

Because it could be an issue with estimating sd or MCSE,
can we skip the error estimates in the mean difference plots
and just do something like a relative difference calculation?

rel_error(a,b) = 2 * abs(a - b) / (abs(a) + abs(b))

- Bob

OK -- I did misunderstand the original. Leading with "May be
a bug" threw me :-) I agree that the increased n_eff
is good.

Daniel just explained what you were doing and we looked
at a couple of cases with big outliers that actually looked
OK. I think the problem is in the plot.

We can't plot differences on a per-sample basis. What we
care about here is

for each parameter,
for each approach,
plot relative error of sample mean vs. known value

where the following should work for relative error:
rel_error(a,b) = 2 * abs(a - b) / (abs(a) + abs(b))

Also, we want to test timing, too. Is there still no way to
get that for v1.3.0?

- Bob

On 5/24/13 10:14 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Things are different. Best that can be said is that the new adaptation takes slightly longer to converge.

Nice plot, not so nice result.

The green seems shifted about 1/2 an e to the right on average,
but up to a whole e to the right at the far end. So it looks
like the new code's taking 50% to 150% longer or so.

If you have the data, could you scatterplot these
by model (ideally with 1.3 on x-axis and 2.0 on the y-axis)?

This is ringing a bell --- Daniel mentioned that the new
code seemed to be more literal in the way it computes leapfrog.
We're not having to compute two gradients per leapfrog
step are we? That is, we can combine the half steps at
the end of one leapfrog step and the beginning of the next?
Or at least save the gradient so we just do the increment
twice?

> I'm not
> going to do anything else until the pull queue clears out and I can run without hacking local branches everywhere.

I was worried the pull queue was going to start slowing
down our work. But I'd think you could just keep going
on your branch and continue to merge in develop branch
as you go.

- Bob

parts:
The green seems shifted about 1/2 an e to the right on average,
but up to a whole e to the right at the far end.  So it looks
like the new code's taking 50% to 150% longer or so.
That is also my impression.

If you have the data, could you scatterplot these
by model (ideally with 1.3 on x-axis and 2.0 on the y-axis)?
The difficulty is that each model has many samples, so there's not a 1-1 correspondence between versions.  I'll have to average, which complicates the scraping a bit.

This is ringing a bell --- Daniel mentioned that the new
code seemed to be more literal in the way it computes leapfrog.
We're not having to compute two gradients per leapfrog
step are we?  That is, we can combine the half steps at
the end of one leapfrog step and the beginning of the next?
Or at least save the gradient so we just do the increment
twice?

Gimme some credit.  ;-)

The steps cannot be combined a la Neal because the NUTS criterion has to be applied between each step.  But the gradient is saved in between iterations, so the only additional overhead is n additions.  My guess is that there are small differences in the acceptance rate/tree depth that might be causing an additional layer to be build, on average.  I need to add more diagnostic plots specific to NUTS.

I was worried the pull queue was going to start slowing
down our work.  But I'd think you could just keep going
on your branch and continue to merge in develop branch
as you go.
The problem is this instance was the reversion, which messed up the mcmc_writer branch and caused a bunch of problems with the diagnostics.
